title: Eve’s Dream and Raphael’s Visit
setting: Eden from dawn to noon; then, in Raphael’s story, Heaven long before the world was made
summary: Eve wakes troubled by a dream in which an angel tempted her to eat the forbidden fruit; Adam comforts her and they sing their morning hymn. God sends Raphael to warn Adam that he is free and that an enemy is coming. Raphael dines with the pair, explains how all creation rises toward spirit, and begins the story of how Satan, jealous of the Son’s exaltation, led a third of the angels into revolt, opposed by Abdiel alone.

sections.title: Adam wakes Eve
sections.note: Adam wakes at dawn, light-headed from pure sleep, and is surprised to find Eve still asleep, flushed and restless. His whispered ‘Awake, my fairest’ echoes the Song of Songs.

sections.title: Eve’s dream
sections.note: Eve tells her dream: a voice like Adam’s called her out by moonlight, an angel ate from the forbidden tree and held the fruit to her mouth, and she flew up above the earth before sinking back. The reader knows it is the whisper Satan breathed into her ear at the end of Book IV.

sections.title: Adam explains dreams
sections.note: Adam gives a short lesson in the mind: when Reason sleeps, Fancy mixes up images into wild work. Evil can pass through the mind and leave no blame if it is not consented to. Eve weeps quietly, and he kisses away the tears.

sections.title: The morning hymn
sections.note: At sunrise Adam and Eve pray, unrehearsed, calling on angels, stars, sun, moon, elements, mists, winds, plants and creatures to praise their Maker. The hymn is modelled on Psalm 148 and ends with a prayer to scatter any evil the night has gathered.

sections.title: God sends Raphael
sections.note: The pair go to work pruning and training vines. God, pitying them, sends the sociable angel Raphael to talk with Adam as friend with friend: to remind him he is free, and to warn him of the enemy so that he cannot later plead surprise.

sections.title: Raphael’s flight to Eden
sections.note: Raphael flies from Heaven’s self-opening gate down through the stars and lands on the eastern cliff of Paradise. Milton compares the far-off earth to the moon seen through Galileo’s telescope and Raphael to the phoenix, then lingers on his six-winged true shape.

sections.title: Preparing for the guest
sections.note: Adam sees the angel coming ‘like another morn risen on mid-noon’ and sends Eve to lay a feast. She plans the courses so that tastes do not clash; Adam walks out to meet his guest with no retinue but his own dignity.

sections.title: Dinner with an angel
sections.note: Raphael greets Eve with the ‘Hail’ later given to Mary, and eats with real hunger, not merely in appearance. He explains that everything created needs feeding, from earth to the stars. Eve, naked and innocent, serves the cups.

sections.title: The scale of nature
sections.note: Adam asks how angelic food compares with earthly. Raphael describes one first matter rising by degrees from body toward spirit, like root to stalk to flower, and hints that obedient men may in time grow wings and rise to Heaven.

sections.title: Free obedience
sections.note: Adam asks what ‘if ye be found obedient’ can mean. Raphael explains that God made him perfect but not unchangeable: service must be free to count, and some angels have already fallen. Adam asks to hear the whole story.

sections.title: The Son proclaimed
sections.note: Raphael begins, warning that he must liken spiritual things to bodily ones. On a day of Heaven’s great year God gathers all the angels and proclaims his Son their head, to whom every knee must bow.

sections.title: Satan’s midnight plot
sections.note: The angels feast and dance until night, but the archangel now called Satan cannot sleep for envy. He wakes his second in command, invents a pretext for marching north, and draws a third of Heaven’s host after him with lies.

sections.title: Father and Son foresee it
sections.note: God sees the revolt and speaks to the Son with grim irony, as though his omnipotence were in danger. The Son, calm, answers that the rebels’ hate will only show his glory.

sections.title: Satan’s speech in the north
sections.note: In his palace on the Mountain of the Congregation, Satan addresses his legions with titles and slogans of liberty: angels are equal and free, and need no anointed king. Notice how persuasive the rhetoric of freedom sounds.

sections.title: Abdiel answers Satan
sections.note: The seraph Abdiel rises alone to rebuke him: God made the angels through the Son, so the Son’s reign honours them. Satan replies that the angels made themselves, ‘self-begot, self-raised’, and threatens to besiege the throne.

sections.title: Abdiel departs alone
sections.note: Unmoved by the roar of applause around him, Abdiel predicts Satan’s ruin and walks out through the hostile host. Milton’s closing lines make him the pattern of a single conscience holding firm against a crowd.

glosses.note: Lustrous, shining like pearls; also ‘eastern’, where the dawn rises.
The morning breeze. Aurora is the Roman goddess of dawn.
The gentle west wind breathing on the goddess of flowers, who in myth was his bride.
The first hour of the day, around sunrise; also the best part of it.
The imagination: the faculty that forms images from what the senses report, for Reason to judge.
Prayers.
Venus as the morning star, the last ‘star’ to fade at dawn.
A group of four: the four elements, earth, water, air and fire, which in old science endlessly change into one another.
In the apocryphal Book of Tobit, Raphael travels in disguise with young Tobias and helps him marry Sarah, whose seven earlier husbands had been killed by a demon on their wedding nights.
Burning ones: the seraphim, whose Hebrew name was understood to mean ‘burning’.
Galileo’s telescope (the ‘glass’) revealed mountains and what seemed seas on the moon. Milton visited him in Italy, and he is the only contemporary named in the poem.
Yielding, pliant; the air gives way to his wings.
A mythical bird, only one alive at a time. The new phoenix carries the remains of the old to the temple of the Sun in Egypt, so all other birds stare at it.
From Isaiah’s vision of the seraphim (Isaiah 6:2), each with six wings: two to cover the face, two the feet, and two to fly.
Hermes, or Mercury, the winged messenger of the gods.
King of the Phaeacians in Homer’s Odyssey, whose orchards bore fruit all year round.
Meads: sweet drinks, here pressed from berries. ‘Must’ is fresh unfermented grape juice.
Pomona is the Roman goddess of fruit trees and orchards.
The judgment of Paris: on Mount Ida, Juno, Minerva and Venus competed naked for the golden apple of the fairest.
The angel Gabriel’s greeting to Mary at the Annunciation (Luke 1:28). Mary was called the ‘second Eve’ because her son would undo Eve’s fall.
The usual explanation of theologians, that angels only seem to eat; in Tobit 12:19 Raphael says his eating was a vision. Milton insists on real hunger.
Genesis 6:2 says the ‘sons of God’ took wives from the daughters of men; many read these as angels.
Reasoning step by step, as humans mostly do; ‘intuitive’ reason grasps truth at once, as angels mostly do.
The ‘great year’ of ancient astronomy: the vast span after which all the heavenly bodies return to their starting positions.
Echoes Psalm 2:7, ‘Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee’. Here it marks the Son’s exaltation as king; he is already at the Father’s side.
Beelzebub, left unnamed here because, as Raphael explains, the rebels’ heavenly names were blotted out.
From Isaiah 14:13, where the fallen ‘Lucifer’ boasts he will sit ‘upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north’.
Revelation 12:4: the dragon’s tail ‘drew the third part of the stars of heaven’.
Psalm 2:9: ‘Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron’.

famous.why: The opening of Adam and Eve’s morning hymn, a joyful paraphrase of the Psalms in which all creation is asked to praise God ‘him first, him last, him midst, and without end’.
Raphael’s image of the plant, root to stalk to leaves to flower, is Milton’s most memorable picture of a universe in which matter and spirit differ in degree, not kind.
‘Freely we serve, / Because we freely love’: the poem’s case for why obedience only counts if it could have been refused.
Satan’s claim that the angels are ‘self-begot, self-raised’ is the root of his rebellion: a refusal to admit he was made.
‘Faithful found / Among the faithless, faithful only he’: Abdiel’s lonely exit is one of the poem’s great portraits of integrity.

themes: Free will: Adam and the angels stand only as long as they freely choose to.
Eve’s dream foreshadows the temptation, and raises the question of how evil can enter an innocent mind.
Heaven and earth are continuous: angels eat, matter rises toward spirit, and Earth may be ‘but a shadow of Heaven’.
Satan speaks the language of liberty and equality; Abdiel answers that true freedom is serving the one who made you.
art: Raphael alighting on the eastern cliff of Paradise in his true form, six wings of gold and sky-blue folded about his shoulders, waist and feet like a mantle.
